vignette:
He is 29, South Asian, and he comes across at first as composed in the careful, practiced way of someone who has learned to keep his face steady while his body stays braced for impact. He owns a small shop, and for years that business has been one of the few places where he feels some measure of control. He knows the rhythm of his days by the sound of the shutter rolling up in the morning, the receipts he counts by hand, the customers who come in for cigarettes, tea, and groceries. He has always taken pride in being reliable, in showing up early, in staying late, in making sure the shelves are full. Before the trauma, he describes himself as patient, social enough, and able to handle pressure.

The violence begins in the relationship he had believed was stable and loving. At first, he minimizes the changes as arguments, jealousy, and harsh words that he thinks he can manage by being more careful, more accommodating, less provoking. But the physical abuse starts to escalate. He describes being pushed, slapped, grabbed by the arms, struck during fights that would begin over ordinary things and end with him trying to make sense of how quickly the person he loved became someone he feared. He remembers the shock of realizing that the abuse is not an isolated moment but a pattern, one that leaves him scanning for the other person's mood before he even opens his mouth. The injury is not only on his skin; it is in the way his confidence erodes with each episode.

After the worst assaults, he becomes preoccupied with escaping and with hiding what is happening. He worries about shame, about what his family might think, about being seen as weak, especially as a man in a community where people are expected to endure quietly. He starts making excuses for bruises and strained movements. When he arrives at the shop, he is often tired from poor sleep and from lying awake replaying the previous night. He keeps working because the shop gives him something to do with his hands, but even there he cannot fully settle. He checks the door repeatedly, startles when customers enter unexpectedly, and feels his muscles tighten whenever he hears footsteps behind him. A raised voice in the street can make his heart hammer so hard that he needs to lean on the counter until it passes.

As the abuse continues, he begins to live as if danger is waiting just around the corner. He avoids situations that might lead to confrontation. He changes routes, delays returning home, and spends longer at the shop than necessary because the thought of being alone with his partner fills him with dread. At night, he sleeps lightly, waking at small sounds. He has nightmares that leave him disoriented and sweating, and he often wakes with his jaw clenched and his body rigid, as if he has been bracing in his sleep. During the day, memories come without warning: the pressure of a hand on his arm, the sound of something hitting the wall, the look on his partner's face just before an outburst. These moments are not experienced as distant recollections but as something that arrives in his body all over again. He feels nauseated, panicked, and suddenly unable to think clearly.

He grows more withdrawn. He stops answering calls from friends as often and declines invitations that once would have been routine. He does not want questions. He does not want pity. He feels increasingly detached, even from people who care about him. At work, he continues to perform, but he does so mechanically, with less attention and less pleasure. He makes mistakes he would not have made before, forgets orders, and finds himself reading the same line on a delivery slip several times. He is frustrated with himself and ashamed of how much effort it takes to appear normal.

By the time he seeks help, he has been living with this fear for a long time. He describes feeling constantly on edge, as if his body no longer believes he is safe anywhere. He is quick to anger and then immediately guilty. He has moments when he feels numb, almost absent, and other moments when memories crash back with such force that he cannot focus on the person speaking to him. Even in the shop, surrounded by familiar goods and familiar faces, he feels a persistent sense that something bad is about to happen. He says he is tired in a way that sleep does not fix, tired of watching the door, tired of flinching, tired of pretending that the life he is living feels like his own.
